desk.explain: Against the US dollar the ringgit moved from 4.1170 to 4.1135 at the 6pm close, a 0.09% move, which is small; Bank Muamalat's economist put it down mainly to technical factors. The bigger overnight force was the US dollar itself: the US 10-year yield slipped to 4.87% from 4.91% and the dollar index eased about 0.10%. The Singapore dollar and euro gained more against the US dollar than the ringgit did, so in ringgit terms SGD rose to 3.1878 from 3.1858 and EUR to 4.5133 from 4.5036; a cross rate is just two US dollar rates divided. On tariffs, the US proposal is up to 18% with 25% possible, MITI calls the rate indicative, and public hearings only start on 25 January 2027, so nothing is final yet.
desk.question: The US just proposed new tariffs on Malaysia, so why did the ringgit strengthen against the US dollar yesterday but weaken against the Singapore dollar and the euro?

headline: Wall Street clawed back most of an AI-led rout and US yields eased, giving Bursa a heavyweight-led bounce and the ringgit a small gain, while a US Section 301 tariff proposal of up to 18% on Malaysian goods now hangs over the market.

learn.answer: EUR/USD = 4.5133 / 4.1135, about 1.0972. With EUR/MYR up and USD/MYR down, the euro must have strengthened against the US dollar.
learn.body: Every ringgit cross is built from two US dollar rates. On Thursday USD/MYR fell to 4.1135 from 4.1170, so the ringgit gained 0.09% on the dollar. SGD/MYR rose to 3.1878 from 3.1858, which means USD/SGD (4.1135 / 3.1878) fell to about 1.2904 from 1.2923, so the Singapore dollar gained about 0.15% on the US dollar, more than the ringgit did. The same arithmetic gives EUR/USD of about 1.0972 (4.5133 / 4.1135), up from about 1.0939. So 'the ringgit strengthened' is only true against the dollar; a customer holding SGD or EUR saw those balances worth more in ringgit.
learn.concept: Cross rates: how the ringgit can rise and fall on the same day
learn.question: If USD/MYR is 4.1135 and EUR/MYR is 4.5133, what EUR/USD rate do they imply, and which way did the euro move against the dollar if EUR/MYR rose while USD/MYR fell?

numbers_note: Only Brent (+3.5%) cleared its move filter outright, and the US 10-year eased 4bp by AP's count (7bp by Bernama's); USD/MYR -0.09%, MGS 10Y -1bp and KLCI +0.56% are small, and the KLCI's fade from 1,584.96 on negative breadth says the bounce was thin.

steps.fact: The S&P 500 fell as much as 3.2% and the Nasdaq as much as 4.6% intraday before closing down 0.3% at 7,182.78 and 0.6% at 23,585.80, with Nvidia down more than 9% at one point and closing 3.9% lower.
The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.87% from 4.91% late Tuesday even though October PCE inflation rose to 3.8% year on year from 3.6%.
Asia rebounded: Hang Seng +1.2% to 22,226.88, Nikkei 225 +0.9% to 57,499.16, Taiex +2.5%, and Kospi +0.3% after a 6.2% drop the day before.

The FBM KLCI rose 8.69 points to 1,570.98 after touching 1,584.96 mid-morning, with Rakuten Trade's Thong Pak Leng crediting easing US Treasury yields, but breadth was negative at 703 losers to 412 gainers.

The ringgit firmed to 4.1135 per US dollar at 6pm from 4.1170, which Bank Muamalat's Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid put down mainly to technical factors, while it slipped against the euro, pound and Singapore dollar.
European shares rallied in early trade, DAX +1.9% to 25,180.12, CAC 40 +1.8% and FTSE 100 +1.6%; closing levels were not confirmed.

The overnight lesson is transmission through yields: a 4bp dip in US 10-year yields lifted Asian risk and nudged USD/MYR down 0.09%, but the KLCI gave back about 14 points from its high and the FBM Emas fell, so this was a bank-and-consumer heavyweight bounce, not a broad turn; with MGS 10Y at 3.78% against UST 4.87%, the -109bp gap means the ringgit still needs a softer dollar rather than carry to gain.

sections.headline: Washington proposed Section 301 tariffs of up to 18% on Malaysian goods, with 25% possible; MITI says it will push to keep the total below 19%.

points.text: USTR proposed tariffs of up to 18% on Malaysian goods on top of existing duties, rising to up to 25% if consultations are judged unsatisfactory, within headline rates of 15–35% for 14 economies.
Written comments are due 5 January 2027 and public hearings begin 25 January 2027; ICT and automotive were named as sectors of particular concern.
MITI said the 18–25% range is only indicative, that Malaysia has no excess manufacturing capacity, and that it will work to keep the total tariff below 19%, with an update by the first quarter.

Because the rate is not final until after late-January hearings, the risk for Bursa's E&E names is a drawn-out overhang rather than a one-day shock; Thursday's tech losers (MI Technovation, ViTrox, UWC) show where sellers lean first.

sections.headline: US inflation is running hotter and a Fed hike is in play, yet yields dipped; BNM stays at 2.75%.

points.text: October's PCE price index rose 3.8% year on year from 3.6%, Q3 GDP was revised up to a 4.3% annual rate, and AP said the Fed is likely to raise rates at its December meeting.
Rakuten Trade's Thong Pak Leng said the US 10-year yield hovered around 4.85% after touching an 11-week low as expectations of more aggressive tightening receded.
BNM held the OPR at 2.75% on 5 November, saying inflation has risen on higher energy costs; the next MPC meeting is 21 January 2027.
With MGS 10Y at 3.78% and UST 10Y at 4.87%, the gap is -109bp; a Fed hike with BNM on hold would widen it, so Thursday's ringgit gain reflects the yield dip, not a closing of the gap.

sections.headline: Brent jumped 3.5% on Middle East supply risk; CPO bounced 1.5% on bargain buying but high stocks cap it.

points.text: Brent rose 3.5% to settle at $94.61 a barrel on Wednesday and has swung between $72 and $114 since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
ING strategists said reports of vessels being targeted in the Strait of Hormuz brought supply risks back into focus.

The third-month February 2027 CPO contract rose RM63 to RM4,292 a tonne; Iceberg X trader David Ng said bargain buying lifted prices but high Malaysian inventories and sluggish exports limited the rebound.
Higher oil supports Malaysia's petroleum revenue and terms of trade, but energy costs are what BNM cites for rising inflation, so oil up is two-edged for MGS yields.
